title: Living ashtpadi 6
hook: every comfort points back to a Giver

segments.voice: Yesterday, dehee: a healthy body, a house, honor kept covered. Your line was by his grace, this home. Did you touch the door frame? Today we live ashtpadi six. Day four hundred sixty-one.

A grandmother is asked how she is, and before any news comes a small phrase: Waheguru di kirpa naal. By Waheguru's grace. The harvest was good, by grace. The grandson passed his exams, by grace. The knee is better, by grace. It can sound like a habit of speech, and partly it is. But habits of speech are where a teaching goes to live. Sukhmani's sixth ashtpadi says jih prasaad, by whose grace, line after line. In homes like hers, the refrain kept going long after the reading ended.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU? BY GRACE.` → `A HABIT OF SPEECH.` → `WHERE A TEACHING GOES TO LIVE.`

segments.voice: Kirpaa is another word for grace, kindness, favor. In ashtpadi four you met it in the child's prayer: in Your kirpaa are countless comforts. Ashtpadi six spreads the same thought across a whole life: food, scent, clothes, house, family, health, honor. Every comfort, a gift. What does it look like to live that, not just read it? Try this. Take one comfort, a hot cup of tea. Trace it back. Someone boiled the water, maybe you. The water came through pipes someone laid, from rain that fell on hills you'll never see. The leaves were picked by hands, maybe in Assam or Kenya or Sri Lanka, by people who got up before dawn. The milk came from an animal someone cared for. The warmth came from fire, or a power line, or the sun. Go back far enough and every comfort runs out of human causes and arrives at something none of us made. That's where Sikh teaching places the Giver: not instead of the farmer and the plumber, but behind and through all of them. Living ashtpadi six means two things at once. Thanks to the people, real thanks, by name if you can. And beneath that, the refrain: jih prasaad. By whose grace any of it exists at all. The grandmother's phrase holds both. The harvest was good because people worked. And by grace.
screen: `KIRPAA: GRACE, KINDNESS, FAVOR.` · `ONE CUP OF TEA, TRACED BACK.` · `PAST THE PEOPLE, TO THE GIVER.` · `THANKS TO BOTH, AT ONCE.` · then, large: `EVERY COMFORT A GIFT.`

segments.voice: The practice: trace one comfort to its source. Choose something you're touching or using right now: the chair, your clothes, the light, the device in your hand. Ask where it came from, and then where that came from. Name the people you pass on the way, even if only as the ones who made it, the ones who carried it. Keep going until you run out of people. Rest there, at the edge of what anyone made. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, or simply sit there grateful. The bell holds the time.
Kirpaa, grace, kindness, favor. Every comfort points back, through many hands, to a Giver: jih prasaad, by whose grace.
Your line: every comfort a gift. Today, thank one person by name for one comfort you usually take for granted, and let the thanks keep going past them. Day four hundred sixty-one.

screen: `DAY 461 COUNTS.` → `ASHTPADI 6, LIVED.` → `TOMORROW: ASHTPADI 7, SALOK: THE HOLY COMPANY.`

howItsDone: In everyday Punjabi speech Sikhs often credit good news to 'Waheguru di kirpa', Waheguru's grace, while also thanking the people involved; ashtpadi six gives that habit its scripture.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kirpaa, grace or kindness; heard in Sukhmani and in everyday Punjabi speech.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'by grace' is just a figure of speech.
what it means: it's ashtpadi six lived out: every comfort points back to a Giver.
what a scholar hears: kirpaa and prasaad are near-synonyms in Gurbani, alongside nadar and karam, other Gurbani words for grace.
